London, Printed for George Nicol, 1790. First edition of Bligh’s account of the Bounty mutiny. The subject of five feature films, hundreds of books, and thousands of articles, the mutiny on the Bounty is the best known incident in maritime history. William Bligh, who had sailed with Cook, was given command of the Bounty to transport breadfruit plants from the Friendly Islands to the West Indies, where it was hoped they would provide a staple food source for the inhabitants. Shortly after the Bounty had left Tahiti in April 1789 the crew, led by the master’s mate, Fletcher Christian, mutinied and set Bligh and eighteen loyal crewmen adrift in a twenty-three foot launch. In their small launch, Bligh and his companions made a remarkable journey of nearly four thousand miles from Tofoa to Timor in six weeks over largely uncharted waters. In the course of this hazardous journey Bligh continued to keep a remarkably detailed and meticulous log in a small notebook and also took the opportunity to chart and name parts of the unknown north-east coast of New Holland as he passed along it – an extraordinary feat of seamanship. description: WALKER, C.B. PHOTOGRAPHS MELBOURNE & SUBURBS by C.B. Walker [cover title]. 35 albumen paper photographic prints, mounted as issued in original photographer's studio album, oblong octavo, original black half, pebble-grain black cloth sides, front board title in gilt, pale tide mark on lower board Melbourne, circa 1890s. Attractive and rare photographic album from the land boom era of ‘Marvellous Melbourne’. Little was known of photographer Charles Bristow Walker’s before the Miegunyah Press publication reproducing an album in the Baillieu Library, University of Melbourne. Ian Morrison edited that publication and has since updated the information on Walker and his album in an article in the journal of the Bibliographical Society of Australia and New Zealand (Script & Print, Vol. 29 (2005), pp. 234-246). It is evident that Walker published the album not as a collection of photographs but more as a ‘binder’ that could be made up as the purchaser wished with either thirty or sixty photographs (or anywhere in between?) and examples of the published albums are known in either form. The combination of images in the few known copies of the album vary the one from the others, which reflect the original owner’s taste and interests. That the physical album was issued more as a binder than a suite of images is supported, for example, by three copies of the album sold by us, one of which had fifty-eight views, six of which were of Sydney, another album of only twenty-two Melbourne views but probably with some – eight? – removed, and the Aitken copy with thirty Melbourne views. The nature of the album as a binder also explains the otherwise slightly puzzling fact that in the known albums, the identifying captions are in manuscript rather than printed. Nine of the thirty-five photos in the current album share a title with ones in Morrison’s book, but all are different (in small or large ways). Provenance: inscribed from architect Sam Brittingham in 1889. Samuel Charles Brittingham was chief architect of the Victorian public works department and was associated with the design of the Old Arts Building (University of Melbourne), the Parkville Post Office, and the Mount Buffalo Chalet. description: MAWSON, Douglas. THE HOME OF THE BLIZZARD: Being the Story of the Australasian Antarctic Expedition, 1911 – 1914. Two volumes, thick octavo, titles printed in two colours, with in total 196 leaves of monochrome plates (including photogravure frontispieces with titling-tissue), seven double-page plates, and two folding plates, eighteen leaves of coloured plates with titling-tissues, and three large folding tinted maps in an end-pocket to Volume II, other illustrations (including maps) in the text , original silver pictorial dark blue cloth, front boards lettered in gilt with a central vignette in silver, titled in the image “Leaning on the Wind”. The classic account of Mawson's first expedition, an epic of endurance which, together with his subsequent work in the Antarctic, forms the most significant basis to Australia's claim to its extensive Antarctic Territory. The expedition charted the entire coastline between the Mertz Glacier and Grassberg, forming the last link in the chain that connected the discoveries of Dumont d'Urville, Wilkes, Scott, and Drygalski. Most importantly, they systematically explored King George V Land and the adjacent Terra Adelie. Mawson's book includes a self-effacing account of his epic journey across five hundred kilometres of Adelie Land in 1912, without a tent and most of his food, one of the great feats of human endurance. Defeated in his main objective, Shackleton was, nonetheless, the first to reach the South Magnetic Pole in the course of this expedition. The narrative was co-written by Shackleton and Edward Saunders, a New Zealand journalist hired by Shackleton as his amanuensis during the return voyage to England.
